name: Oracle VirtualBox
license: GPLv3 for the base package and Guest Additions (GPLv2 before 7.0); the optional Extension Pack is proprietary: free under the PUEL for personal and educational use, a paid Enterprise license otherwise
summary: Oracle’s free, open-source desktop hypervisor: a type-2 hypervisor that runs VMs as an application on Windows, macOS, Linux and Solaris, scriptable with `VBoxManage` and the default provider for Vagrant.
intro: VirtualBox is a hosted (type 2) hypervisor: it installs like any other application on an existing operating system and runs virtual machines beside your normal programs, unlike a bare-metal hypervisor that owns the hardware. On x86_64 it runs on Windows, Linux, Intel Macs and Oracle Solaris and hosts x86 and x86_64 guests such as Windows, Linux and Solaris. Version 7.1 (September 2024) added Apple silicon Macs and 7.2 (August 2025) Windows on Arm, but an Arm host runs only Arm guests: 64-bit Arm Linux and Windows 11 for Arm, not x86 systems. Each VM is an XML settings file plus disk images (VDI, VMDK or VHD), the same on every host, so a VM made on Windows runs on Linux, and VMs move between products as OVF appliances. On a Windows host where Hyper-V is on, VirtualBox uses Hyper-V as its virtualization engine, which the manual warns can slow VMs down significantly.

You drive it from the VirtualBox Manager GUI or from `VBoxManage`, which can do everything the GUI does: create and modify VMs, attach disks, run an unattended OS install, take and restore snapshots, and start VMs headless with no window. Installing the Guest Additions inside a guest adds drivers for mouse integration, automatic resizing and better video, shared folders, a shared clipboard, drag and drop, seamless windows and time sync. Each VM gets up to eight virtual network cards (four in the GUI), each in its own mode: NAT, the default, where the guest reaches out but nothing reaches in without port forwarding; NAT Network; bridged onto the physical LAN; host-only; internal (VMs only); and a few rarer modes. Vagrant uses VirtualBox as its default provider.

The base package, including the Guest Additions, has been GPLv3 since 7.0 (October 2022), a switch Oracle made for compatibility with the license of Qt 5.7 and later. The optional Extension Pack adds the VRDP remote display server, host webcam passthrough, an Intel PXE boot ROM, AES disk image encryption and Oracle Cloud integration, and is not open source. Its PUEL license covers personal and educational use only and excludes any use to run a business, organization, government body or school; that needs an Enterprise license, which Oracle sells for named workstation users in a minimum quantity of 100. The current release is 7.2.20 (September 22, 2026); the 7.2 branch has had eight maintenance releases so far in 2026, and the older 7.1 branch still got 7.1.18 in April 2026.
strengths: Free and open source (GPLv3), on all major desktop operating systems, with VM files that move between hosts unchanged
Good desktop integration through the Guest Additions: shared folders, clipboard, drag and drop, automatic resizing, seamless windows
Fully scriptable: `VBoxManage` covers every GUI action, including unattended installs, headless start and snapshots, and it is the interface Vagrant drives
Branched snapshot trees: save a VM’s state, go back to any snapshot and start an alternative configuration from there
Per-NIC networking modes, from simple NAT to bridged, host-only and internal networks, cover most local lab topologies
limits: A desktop tool, not a server platform: VMs run on top of a general-purpose host OS, and the manual warns not to run another hypervisor’s VMs at the same time because it can crash the host; with Hyper-V on, VirtualBox runs on top of it and can be much slower
On Apple silicon and Windows on Arm it runs only Arm guests (Linux and Windows 11), no x86 systems; 3D acceleration on Arm Macs is experimental, and Arm VMs saved in 7.1 can’t be resumed in 7.2

The Extension Pack is proprietary: the PUEL forbids business, government and school use, the Enterprise license comes in a minimum of 100 named users, 7.1 removed the PUEL’s evaluation clause, and the binaries may not be redistributed
Oracle gives Premier support only for selected guests (recent Windows, Oracle Linux and Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Solaris); Ubuntu, SUSE, older Windows and others get limited support only

story: VirtualBox began at innotek, a privately funded company in Stuttgart, Germany, with offices in Dresden and Berlin, that had worked on PC virtualization since 2001. It first sold VirtualBox under a proprietary license. On January 15, 2007 innotek made version 1.3.2 free software under the GPL, while still selling an enterprise variant with extra features and support under a proprietary license.

Sun Microsystems announced on February 12, 2008 that it would buy innotek, citing more than four million downloads since January 2007, and completed the purchase on February 20 to bring VirtualBox into its xVM family as the desktop counterpart to xVM Server. Oracle completed its acquisition of Sun on January 27, 2010, and VirtualBox became an Oracle product. VirtualBox 4.0, in December 2010, reorganized the software into an open-source base package and separately licensed Extension Packs.

Oracle moved the base package from GPLv2 to GPLv3 for VirtualBox 7.0 in October 2022, because newer Qt versions required it. Version 7.1 in September 2024 brought Arm virtualization to Apple silicon Macs, and 7.2 in August 2025 added Windows on Arm hosts and moved the NVMe controller emulation into the open-source base package.

choices.choice: An open-source base with a proprietary add-on
choices.why: innotek opened the core under the GPL in 2007 but kept selling extra features. Since 4.0 those features live in a separately licensed Extension Pack, so the base package can be freely redistributed while Oracle charges businesses for the extras.

choices.choice: A hosted hypervisor rather than bare metal
choices.why: VirtualBox targets developers’ laptops and desktops: it runs alongside existing applications and uses the same file formats on every host OS, so a VM moves between Windows, macOS and Linux machines.

Emulated hardware alone gives only basic video and a captured mouse. The Guest Additions, installed in the guest, add the integration desktop users expect: seamless mouse, resizing, shared folders and clipboard.
The commit that changed the license files in August 2022 says GPLv3 was required for compatibility with the license of Qt 5.7 and later, which the GUI uses.
